title: The five elements and how to classify items
summary: The IASB definitions of assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses, the governing equation, how net profit links the two statements, and the 30-item classification worksheet with its tricky ones.

chunks.heading: Five elements, one equation
chunks.explanation_md:
The **IASB Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting** says every financial statement item can be traced to one of **five elements**: **assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses**.

They hang together through the **governing equation**:

**Assets = Liabilities + Equity**

The five split into two groups:

- **Assets, liabilities and equity** are **balance sheet (position) elements**, measured **at a point in time**.
- **Income and expenses** are **income statement (performance) elements**, measured **over a period**.

The thread that connects the two statements: **net profit or loss (income minus expenses) flows into retained earnings, which is part of equity.**

key_terms.meaning: Assets, liabilities and equity: balance sheet items measured at a point in time.
Income and expenses: income statement items measured over a period.

chunks.exam_line: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Assets, liabilities, equity: balance sheet, point in time. Income, expenses: income statement, over a period. Net profit flows into retained earnings, part of equity.

chunks.heading: The five definitions, word by word
chunks.explanation_md:
Learn these closely: every classification question comes back to them.

- **Assets:** a **present economic resource controlled by the entity** as a result of **past events**, with the **potential to produce economic benefits**.
- **Liabilities:** a **present obligation** of the entity to **transfer an economic resource** as a result of past events.
- **Equity:** the **residual interest** in the assets of the entity **after deducting all its liabilities**.
- **Income:** **increases in assets, or decreases in liabilities**, resulting in **increases in equity** (other than **owner contributions**). Includes **revenues and gains**.
- **Expenses:** **decreases in assets, or increases in liabilities**, resulting in **decreases in equity** (other than **owner distributions**). Includes **expenses and losses**.

Notice the mirror: income and expenses are defined by what they do to assets, liabilities and equity, and money owners put in or take out is kept out of both.

chunks.heading: Practice worksheet: assets and liabilities
chunks.explanation_md:
The practice worksheet gives **30 items** to classify as **A (Asset), L (Liability), E (Equity), I (Income) or Ex (Expense)**. Try each one before checking the answer key. Here is how the answer key sorts them.

**Assets:**
- Building owned by the company
- Goodwill
- Trade receivables (debtors)
- Patent rights
- Insurance premium paid (prepaid)
- Closing stock / Inventory
- Cash in hand
- Investment in shares of another company

**Liabilities:**
- Salaries payable to employees
- Bank overdraft
- Advance received from customer (unearned revenue)
- Long-term bank loan
- Bonds payable
- Outstanding electricity bill (accrued expense)
chunks.exam_line: Prepaid insurance, goodwill and patent rights are assets; bank overdraft, an advance from a customer and an outstanding bill are liabilities.

check_questions.stem: On the answer key, 'Insurance premium paid (prepaid)' is:
Which of these is a liability on the answer key?
Goodwill is classified as an asset.

chunks.heading: Practice worksheet: equity, income and expenses
chunks.explanation_md:
**Equity:**
- Share capital issued to shareholders
- General reserve
- Dividend paid to shareholders
- Retained earnings / Accumulated profits

**Income:**
- Interest earned on fixed deposit
- Rent received from tenant
- Revenues from operation/Sales
- Discount received from supplier
- Gain on foreign currency translation

**Expenses:**
- Depreciation on machinery
- Sales commission expense
- Loss on sale of investment
- Bad debts written off
- Interest expense on loan
- Repair and maintenance expense
- Purchase of Goods/Cost of Goods Sold

Gains sit with **income** and losses sit with **expenses**, exactly as the definitions say: income includes revenues and gains, expenses include expenses and losses.
chunks.exam_line: General reserve and dividend paid are equity; discount received and gain on foreign currency translation are income; loss on sale of investment and bad debts written off are expenses.

chunks.heading: The tricky ones
chunks.explanation_md:
The answer key adds notes on the items that trip people up:

- **#9, advance received from customer (unearned revenue): liability.** It is an **obligation not yet fulfilled**: the goods or service are still owed. Contrast it with **#14, revenues from operation/sales**, which is **income already earned**.
- **#16, dividend paid to shareholders: equity.** It is a **distribution of profit to owners, not a cost of earning it**. It **reduces equity directly and never hits the income statement**.
- **#27, outstanding electricity bill (accrued expense): liability.** The **expense has already been recognised on the income statement**; what remains is the **unpaid obligation**.

Each note goes back to the definitions: a liability is a present obligation, and expenses exclude owner distributions.
chunks.exam_line: Unearned revenue: liability (still owed). Dividend paid: reduces equity directly, never the income statement. Outstanding bill: liability (expense already recognised, obligation unpaid).

questions.stem: Differentiate between item #9, an advance received from a customer, and item #14, revenues from operation/sales, on the practice worksheet.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both items involve customers, but the answer key puts them in different elements.

| Point | #9 Advance from customer | #14 Revenues from operation/Sales |
|---|---|---|
| Element | **Liability** | **Income** |
| Why | An **obligation not yet fulfilled**: the goods or service are still owed | **Income already earned** |
| Link to definition | A present obligation to transfer an economic resource | An increase in assets that raises equity |
| Statement | Balance sheet | Income statement |

**Conclusion:** the test is whether the business has delivered; until it does, money received in advance is owed back as goods or service, so it is a liability.

rubric.point: #9 is a liability; #14 is income
#9: obligation not yet fulfilled, goods or service still owed
#14: income already earned

questions.stem: Why does the answer key treat item #16, dividend paid to shareholders, as equity and not as an expense?
questions.model_answer_md:
This is one of the tricky items flagged in the answer key notes.

- A dividend is a **distribution of profit to owners, not a cost of earning it**.
- So it **reduces equity directly** and **never hits the income statement**.
- This follows the definition of expenses: decreases in equity **other than owner distributions**.

**Conclusion:** expenses are costs of earning income; payments to owners are kept out of them and shown as a reduction of equity.

rubric.point: Distribution of profit to owners, not a cost of earning it
Reduces equity directly, never hits income statement
Expenses definition excludes owner distributions

questions.stem: Explain how net profit connects the income statement and the balance sheet, according to the session.
questions.model_answer_md:
The session calls this the thread that connects the two statements.

- **Assets, liabilities and equity** are balance sheet (position) elements, measured **at a point in time**.
- **Income and expenses** are income statement (performance) elements, measured **over a period**.
- **Net profit or loss = income minus expenses**, and it **flows into retained earnings**, which is **part of equity**.

So the governing equation, **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**, still holds after the period's profit is added.

**Conclusion:** performance over the period changes the position at the end of it through retained earnings.

rubric.point: Position elements at a point in time; performance elements over a period
Net profit = income minus expenses
Net profit flows into retained earnings, part of equity

questions.stem: State and explain the five elements of financial statements as defined in the IASB Conceptual Framework, and show how they fit together.
questions.model_answer_md:
The **IASB Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting** says every financial statement item can be traced to one of **five elements**.

**The definitions**
- **Assets:** a **present economic resource controlled by the entity** as a result of **past events**, with the **potential to produce economic benefits**. Example from the worksheet: building owned by the company.
- **Liabilities:** a **present obligation** to **transfer an economic resource** as a result of past events. Example: long-term bank loan.
- **Equity:** the **residual interest** in the assets after deducting all liabilities. Example: share capital issued to shareholders.
- **Income:** increases in assets or decreases in liabilities that **increase equity**, other than owner contributions. It **includes revenues and gains**. Example: rent received from tenant.
- **Expenses:** decreases in assets or increases in liabilities that **decrease equity**, other than owner distributions. It **includes expenses and losses**. Example: loss on sale of investment.

**How they fit together**
- The **governing equation**: **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**.
- Assets, liabilities and equity are **balance sheet (position)** elements, measured at a **point in time**.
- Income and expenses are **income statement (performance)** elements, measured **over a period**.
- **Net profit or loss (income minus expenses) flows into retained earnings**, part of equity, which ties the two statements together.

**Conclusion:** learn the definitions closely, because every classification question, like the 30-item worksheet, comes back to them.

questions.stem: Classify the following worksheet items into the five elements and justify the tricky ones: building owned by the company; salaries payable to employees; general reserve; discount received from supplier; insurance premium paid (prepaid); bank overdraft; dividend paid to shareholders; gain on foreign currency translation; outstanding electricity bill (accrued expense); depreciation on machinery; investment in shares of another company; advance received from customer (unearned revenue).
questions.model_answer_md:
Each item is tested against the five definitions, as in the practice worksheet.

| Item | Element |
|---|---|
| Building owned by the company | Asset |
| Salaries payable to employees | Liability |
| General reserve | Equity |
| Discount received from supplier | Income |
| Insurance premium paid (prepaid) | Asset |
| Bank overdraft | Liability |
| Dividend paid to shareholders | Equity |
| Gain on foreign currency translation | Income |
| Outstanding electricity bill (accrued expense) | Liability |
| Depreciation on machinery | Expense |
| Investment in shares of another company | Asset |
| Advance received from customer (unearned revenue) | Liability |

**Justifying the tricky ones**
- **Advance from customer:** an **obligation not yet fulfilled**; the goods or service are still owed, so it is a liability, unlike sales, which is income already earned.
- **Dividend paid:** a **distribution of profit to owners, not a cost of earning it**; it reduces equity directly and never hits the income statement.
- **Outstanding electricity bill:** the **expense has already been recognised** on the income statement; what remains is the **unpaid obligation**, a liability.
- **Prepaid insurance:** cash paid in advance for a benefit still to come, so it is an asset.
- **Gain on foreign currency translation:** income **includes gains**, just as expenses include losses.

**Conclusion:** ask whether the item is something owned, something owed, the owners' claim, or a change in equity from performance; owner payouts and unfulfilled obligations are the usual traps.

rubric.point: Assets: building, prepaid insurance, investment in shares
Liabilities: salaries payable, overdraft, electricity bill, customer advance
Equity: general reserve, dividend paid; Income: discount received, currency gain; Expense: depreciation
Customer advance: obligation not yet fulfilled
Dividend: distribution to owners, reduces equity directly
Outstanding bill: expense recognised, unpaid obligation remains
